prompt: Right after linking `node` into `~/.local/bin`, `node --version` said `command not found`. Why?
hint: The fix was to open a new terminal.

choices.text: The tarball was for the wrong processor
choices.why: `uname -m` said `x86_64` and the file taken was `linux-x64`; a wrong file would fail differently, and a new terminal would not fix it.

choices.text: A terminal adds `~/.local/bin` to its `PATH` only if the folder existed when it opened
choices.why: Right. This terminal was opened before the folder existed, so it never searches there.

choices.text: The links in `~/.local/bin` need `sudo` before they run
choices.why: Nothing in the setup used `sudo` for Node; it lives in your home and touches nothing else.

choices.text: npm has to be set up first
choices.why: npm came in the same tarball and failed the same way; the order of the two is not the problem.

prompt: What did `--save-exact` change in `~/vue-tools/package.json`?
hint: Compare the `playwright` line with how create-vue wrote Vue's.

choices.text: It also downloaded Chromium into the project
choices.why: The browser is a separate download of about 300 MB, fetched by `npx playwright install`.

choices.text: It made npm refuse any Playwright newer than the one on the registry today
choices.why: It writes nothing about the registry; it fixes the version in the file, so the next install reads the same number.

choices.text: It wrote `1.63.0` rather than `^1.63.0`
choices.why: Right. Without the caret a later install cannot pick a newer Playwright, and a transcript stays true.

choices.text: It saved Playwright under `devDependencies`
choices.why: The file shows it under `dependencies`; `--save-exact` is about the version, not the group.

prompt: A virtual machine running Ubuntu Server has no browser window, so the command ___ is how you see a page there.
hint: The small program this section writes, in four letters.

prompt: create-vue wrote `"vue": "^3.5.42"`. Which versions does that allow?
hint: The caret is the convenience npm chose by default.

choices.text: Only 3.5.42
choices.why: That is what the course writes, with no caret: `3.5.44` and nothing else.

choices.text: 3.5.42 and later patches of 3.5, but never 3.6
choices.why: That is a narrower range than the caret gives; `^` lets the minor number move too.

choices.text: Any version up to 3.5.42
choices.why: The caret points upwards: it is a floor, not a ceiling.

choices.text: 3.5.42 or any later 3.x
choices.why: Right. Two installs a month apart get two different Vues if one came out in between, which is why the course pins it.

prompt: Which of these did the course change in what create-vue wrote? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three files were replaced, each for its own reason.

choices.text: It removed vite-plugin-vue-devtools
choices.why: Right. It fills every page with requests and a button that have nothing to do with your code.

choices.text: It switched the project to TypeScript
choices.why: The opposite: naming `--prettier` instead of `--default` kept it JavaScript; TypeScript is lesson 16.

choices.text: It gave `index.html` a `lang` and a real title
choices.why: Right. `lang="en"` tells a screen reader which voice to use, and create-vue left it empty.

choices.text: It took the `@` alias out of `vite.config.js`
choices.why: The alias stayed; only the line loading the devtools plugin went.

choices.text: It pinned every package to an exact version
choices.why: Right. No caret is left, so the install fetches what the course recorded.

prompt: Why does the course run `npm create vue@3.24.0 -- --prettier --bare planner` rather than `npm create vue` with no options?
hint: With no options it asks; with `--default` it picks a language.

choices.text: Vite refuses to start a project that has no formatter
choices.why: Vite does not know Prettier exists; `npm run dev` runs `vite`, and `format` is a separate script.

choices.text: Naming one feature skips the questions, and gives JavaScript where `--default` gives TypeScript
choices.why: Right. Prettier is the cheapest feature to name, and `--bare` leaves out the example components.

choices.text: `--prettier` pins every version
choices.why: Pinning was done afterwards, by hand, in `package.json`; create-vue still wrote carets.

choices.text: Without options it writes no `package.json`
choices.why: Every project create-vue writes has one; the options change what is in it, not whether it exists.

prompt: What is `package-lock.json` for, and what should you do with it?
hint: `npm ls` showed four names; the lockfile knows more.

choices.text: It records the exact version of every package in the tree; commit it
choices.why: Right. It includes the ones you never named, so the next `npm install` on any machine fetches the same tree.

choices.text: It is a copy of `node_modules`, so a clone of the project needs no install
choices.why: `node_modules` is rebuilt from the lockfile and never stored; a fresh clone has none.

choices.text: It lists the four packages of `package.json` again; delete it
choices.why: Four is what `npm ls` shows at the top; the install added 36 packages and the lockfile has every one.

choices.text: It stops a second `npm install` from running; keep it out of git
choices.why: It does the opposite of stopping one: it makes every later install reproduce the first.

prompt: A friend clones your planner from git, runs `npm run dev` and gets `sh: 1: vite: not found`. What is wrong?
hint: Ask what a clone carries and what it does not.

choices.text: Their Node is older than 22.18
choices.why: An old Node is worth checking first in general, but `vite: not found` says the program itself is missing from `node_modules/.bin`.

choices.text: Vite was installed globally on your machine and not on theirs
choices.why: Nothing here installs Vite globally; npm looks for it in the project's own `node_modules/.bin`.

choices.text: No `node_modules`: a clone never has one until `npm install` runs
choices.why: Right. It is rebuilt from the lockfile rather than stored, so the first step after a clone is `npm install`.

choices.text: They ran it outside the project's folder
choices.why: That gives `Could not read package.json`; here npm found the script `dev`, so it was standing in the right place.

prompt: A second `npm run dev` started while the first was running. At which port did Vite serve the page?
hint: It said `Port 5173 is in use` and took the next one.

prompt: The page went blank after you saved a change to `App.vue`. Where do you look first?
hint: The explanation of the `` was not in the browser.

choices.text: The browser's console
choices.why: That is the second place; in the lesson's case it said almost nothing.

choices.text: `node_modules`, and reinstall it in case a package broke
choices.why: Nothing was wrong with the packages; a template had a mistake, and reinstalling would not touch it.

choices.text: The text `look` prints of `#app`
choices.why: It was empty, which tells you the page is blank and not why.

choices.text: The terminal running the dev server
choices.why: Right. It named the error, the file, the line and the column, with a caret under the character.

prompt: What does the browser receive when it asks the dev server for `/src/App.vue`?
hint: The `curl` in this section asked the same question.

choices.text: The `.vue` file as written, which Vue parses in the page
choices.why: The browser has never heard of the format; the Vue plugin inside Vite turns it into JavaScript first.

choices.text: A JS module with a render function
choices.why: Right. `_sfc_render` is that function, and running it builds the page.

choices.text: HTML with holes in it, which Vue fills in afterwards
choices.why: That is the common wrong picture the section names: the template is compiled, not filled in.

choices.text: Finished HTML, rendered by Vite on the server
choices.why: Vite compiled the file; the elements themselves are built in the browser, by running the function.

prompt: In the compiled `App.vue`, the heading is written `_cache[0] || (_cache[0] = _createElementVNode("h1", …))`. What does that say?
hint: Is there anything in that heading that ever changes?

choices.text: The browser keeps the file in its HTTP cache
choices.why: This is a variable inside the render function, not a response header; it is about the node, not the file.

choices.text: Vite saved the compiled module to disk
choices.why: Vite does keep things on disk, but `_cache` is in the code the browser runs, and it holds a virtual node.

choices.text: Nothing in it ever changes, so it is made once and reused
choices.why: Right. The compiler read the template and found it static; `-1 /* CACHED */` tells the runtime the same.

choices.text: The heading is rebuilt on each render and compared with the old one before it is drawn
choices.why: That is what the `||` avoids: once `_cache[0]` holds the node, the call after it never runs again.

prompt: Which of these are true of a single-file component? Choose all that apply.
hint: The table of blocks says how many of each.

choices.text: It has at most one `<template>`
choices.why: Right. One block of markup per component.

choices.text: Its blocks have to come in the order script, template, style
choices.why: That order is a recommendation, because it reads top to bottom; the order is yours to choose.

choices.text: It has room for several `<style>` blocks
choices.why: Right. As many as you like, scoped or not.

choices.text: Its `<script setup>` runs once for each copy of the component
choices.why: Right. Every copy on the screen gets its own state.

choices.text: A browser opens it directly, without a compiler
choices.why: That is the cost of the format: there is always a compiler between you and the page.

prompt: In `src/main.js`, `createApp(App).___('#app')` hands the application the `<div id="app">` of `index.html`.
hint: The method that attaches an application to an element.

prompt: Why is the footer component called `AppFooter` rather than `Footer`?
hint: Think of the elements HTML has, and the ones it will have.

choices.text: Vue only finds components whose name starts with `App`
choices.why: `App` is just this project's prefix; any two-word PascalCase name would do.

choices.text: One-word names collide with HTML elements, present or future
choices.why: Right. `<footer>` is already one, and the Vue style guide asks for two words.

choices.text: `Footer` is a reserved word in JavaScript
choices.why: It is not; the clash is with HTML's elements, not with the language.

choices.text: A file name in PascalCase needs two capitals before Vite will compile it
choices.why: Vite compiles any `.vue` file; the two words are a convention of the style guide.

prompt: In `App.vue` the markup reads `courses.length`, and the setup block only says `const courses = [...]`. Why is that enough?
hint: Compare it with the page in "A page at a time", which had to do more.

choices.text: Because `courses` is exported with `export default`
choices.why: There is no export in that script at all; nothing more than the `const` is written.

choices.text: Because a fixed list has to be a `ref` and Vue wraps it for you
choices.why: Nothing is wrapped; the list is fixed text until lesson 2 makes it reactive.

choices.text: Because Vue puts every variable of the page in scope for every template
choices.why: Only what the component's own `<script setup>` declares is visible; another file's `const` is not.

choices.text: Anything declared at the top of `<script setup>` is visible to the template by name
choices.why: Right. No `return` and no export: the long form, `setup()` returning an object, is what it saves you.

prompt: `AppFooter.vue` has a scoped rule for `p`. What selector did the stylesheet Vite sent actually contain?
hint: The `curl` of the style block printed it.

choices.why: That would match any paragraph inside a stamped element, children's included; the attribute went on the `p` itself.

choices.text: `.AppFooter p`
choices.why: No class is added; Vue marks elements with a `data-v-` attribute instead.

choices.text: `p`, unchanged, with each footer paragraph given an inline style
choices.why: Nothing is inlined; the rule is rewritten and the browser runs ordinary CSS.
Right. A paragraph, and only one carrying this component's attribute.

prompt: You write rules in `App.vue`'s `<style scoped>`. Which of these reach an element that `AppFooter` drew? Choose all that apply.
hint: One leak comes from where the child's root sits; the other is said out loud.

choices.text: A plain rule for `p`, aimed at the footer's paragraph
choices.why: That is the case scoping exists for: the footer's `p` carries only `AppFooter`'s attribute, so the rule misses it.

choices.text: A plain rule for `footer`
choices.why: Right. `<footer>` is the child's root, and a root gets the parent's attribute too, so a parent can place its children.

choices.text: A rule using `:deep(p)` under an element of `App.vue` that contains the footer
choices.why: Right. The attribute goes on the outer selector and `p` is left bare, so it matches inside a child too.

choices.text: Any rule at all, because both files are in one page
choices.why: In plain CSS that would be so, and it is exactly what the attributes prevent.

prompt: Why does scoped style cost nothing at run time?
hint: Who did the work, and when?

choices.text: The compiler did the work; the browser runs plain CSS
choices.why: Right. It stamped the elements and rewrote the selectors before the page ever loaded.

choices.text: Each component is put inside its own Shadow DOM, which the browser isolates for free
choices.why: No shadow root appears in the footer's HTML; the isolation is two attributes meeting a selector.

choices.text: Vue checks the rules against each element after a render, but only for scoped blocks
choices.why: Nothing in Vue's runtime looks at CSS; the browser matches the rules as it does for any stylesheet.

choices.text: Vite writes the rules into every element's `style`
choices.why: The footer's HTML has `data-v-` attributes and no `style`; the rules stay in a stylesheet.

prompt: What does Vue's documentation mean by calling Vue a *progressive* framework?
hint: What did the study-group page keep, and what did it give Vue?

choices.text: It loads a page's components bit by bit, as the reader scrolls
choices.why: That is lazy loading, a different idea; the word here is about adopting Vue, not loading it.

choices.text: It upgrades itself through each minor version
choices.why: Versions are pinned in this course precisely so that nothing upgrades itself.

choices.text: It takes over one element of an existing page and leaves the rest alone
choices.why: Right. A widget at a time, on a page a server already renders, with no build step.

choices.text: Its templates are compiled in stages by the dev server
choices.why: In this section there is no dev server at all; the template is compiled in the browser.

prompt: `vue.esm-browser.prod.js` is 175 kB and the runtime build without the compiler is 113 kB. How many kB of the first is the compiler?
hint: The section rounds it.

prompt: Why does the study-group page need `python3 -m http.server` instead of being opened from disk?
hint: Look at the first line of its `<script type="module">`.

choices.text: Python compiles the template before the browser sees it
choices.why: The server only hands over files; the template is compiled by Vue, in the browser.

choices.text: A page opened from disk cannot import a module
choices.why: Right. The `import` from `./vue.esm-browser.prod.js` needs the page served over HTTP.

choices.text: A button with `@click` does nothing on a page whose address starts with `file:`
choices.why: The click handler is fine; it is the script never loading Vue that would leave it dead.

choices.text: `look` reads only `localhost` addresses
choices.why: `look` opens whatever URL it is given; the limit is the browser's, for modules on disk.

prompt: Put these steps in the order that took the planner from nothing to a page `look` could print.
hint: The dev server needs installed packages, and the packages need a pinned `package.json`.
items: Start `npm run dev` in a second terminal

prompt: Somebody adds Vue to a server-rendered page the way "A page at a time" did, but copies the smaller `vue.runtime.esm-browser.prod.js` to save 62 kB. What happens to the counter?
hint: Which of the two files carries the compiler, and who else could compile that template?

choices.text: It works the same, just 62 kB lighter
choices.why: The 62 kB that were saved are the compiler, and the template inside `#counter` still needs compiling.

choices.text: The browser's HTML parser turns the template into a render function instead
choices.why: The browser parses it as HTML, and that is all: braces and `@click` mean nothing to it.

choices.text: Vite compiles it on the next save
choices.why: There is no Vite here; this page has no build and no dev server.

choices.text: Nothing compiles the template in the page, so the counter does not work
choices.why: Right. With no build, the compiler has to travel to the browser; the runtime build is for templates compiled beforehand.

prompt: Which of these happen on your machine rather than in the browser, in the planner as this lesson built it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Follow `App.vue` from the file on disk to the elements on the screen.

choices.text: Rewriting `p` as `p[data-v-6704560a]`
choices.why: Right. The compiler rewrote the selector before the stylesheet was sent.

choices.text: Turning the template into `_sfc_render`
choices.why: Right. The Vue plugin inside Vite compiles the file on the dev server.

choices.text: Making virtual nodes out of `_createElementVNode` calls
choices.why: Those calls run when the render function runs, and that is in the browser.
